headline: Peconic's summer clock strikes porgy season — Shelter Island humps loaded, bass gone nocturnal
subhead: The bay warmed early again this year, and now it's paying out porgies by the dozen while stripers wait for dark to feed.
body_markdown:
By the second week of July the Peconic has usually settled into its summer groove, and this year is no exception — if anything it got there a touch early. The bay always heats faster than the Sound because it's shallower and more enclosed, and that head start shows up every summer in the same order: porgies first, fluke tucked into the channels once the flats get too warm for them, and stripers sliding onto the night shift as the surface temps climb into the mid-70s. That's exactly the pattern we're in right now.

Start with the porgies, because that's where the easy, honest fun is this week. The humps around Shelter Island — the drop east of Jennys Point, the rocky patches off Cedar Island, and the bar running out from Hay Beach — are holding thick porgy schools in 15 to 25 feet. High-low rigs with size 6 or 8 hooks, half a sandworm or a chunk of skimmer clam, fished on the bottom during the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing. That current-edge window is when the porgies really turn on and feed with confidence instead of picking. Anchor up rather than drift here — porgies want that bait sitting still on structure, not swimming past. Guys working these humps this week have had steady action, fish running 10 to 13 inches with enough 14s mixed in to make it worth culling for the pan. This is about as reliable as fishing gets on the East End right now, and it should hold through August as long as the water stays clean.

Fluke have done what fluke always do once the shallow bay water pushes past 70 — they've pulled off the open flats and settled into the channels where there's moving water and a little more oxygen. Noyack Bay channel, the Shelter Island Sound drop along the ferry route, and the deeper cut off Cedar Point have all been holding fish in 18 to 35 feet. The bite is honest but not a bonanza — you're covering ground to find the pockets. White or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the tide pushing you through the deeper water, has been the most consistent combination. Best window is the two hours around the tide change, when the current slows enough to keep the bait in the strike zone instead of racing past it. Fish are mostly in the 16 to 19 inch range with keepers mixed in — nothing to write home about size-wise, but enough action to make an afternoon worthwhile if you're willing to move around and not just sit on one drift.

Stripers are the honest disappointment of the week if you're fishing daylight hours, and I'll say it straight — the bay's warm enough now that the bass have mostly gone nocturnal. Regional water temps back that up; the Sound and ocean side are both sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and the Peconic's shallower water is likely running a couple degrees warmer than that on a sunny afternoon. Bass don't like feeding hard in that kind of warmth during the day, so the smart money has shifted to the last hour of light and into full dark. Orient Point and the rip off Plum Gut are still throwing bass after sundown, working eels or bunker chunks on the outgoing tide when the current rips through that gut and disorients the bait. Gardiners Bay has some bunker schools moving through, and where you find those pods, there are bluefish underneath them tearing them apart — that's been a daytime bite worth chasing if you spot the surface commotion. Bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig, or a diamond jig worked through the melee, will connect. Bluefish have been the more dependable daytime target the last couple weeks while the bass sulk in the heat.

Weakfish are showing in small numbers around Three Mile Harbor and the mouth of Northwest Harbor — nothing to build a trip around, but a nice bonus if you're working soft plastics in that zone for something else. A few 18 to 22 inch fish have turned up on light jigs fished near the bottom on the last of the ebb.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change dramatically this week unless we get a real cool-down or a strong blow to mix the water. The moon's past new and building toward the first quarter, which means tidal push is moderate rather than extreme — good for the porgy bite, which doesn't need a hard current to produce, but it also means the fluke channels won't get the strong flush that sometimes triggers a better bite. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd spend the morning on the Shelter Island porgy grounds while the tide's right, then switch over to Orient Point or the Gut for the evening bass and blues as the light fades. That combination — daytime porgies, evening bass — is about as solid a read on this bay as you'll get in mid-July. Keep an eye on the bait schools in Gardiners Bay too; if the bunker stick around, the blues and the occasional bass working them during daylight could turn into the best action of the week.
